Article Title: FIR against Prashant Bhushan for sharing fake video of Russian minister criticising India
Article Text:
FIR against Prashant Bhushan for sharing fake video of Russian minister criticising India

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

An FIR has been registered against senior advocate Prashant Bhushan for sharing a morphed video purportedly showing Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov criticising India over its internal affairs and oil purchases.The development comes a day after the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) fact-checked the video, confirming that the clip was fabricated. The clarification followed a denial by the Russian Embassy, which also disputed the authenticity of the video.Bhushan had shared the clip on social media with the caption, "a tight slap by the Russian foreign minister on India. What kind of advice was Jaishankar giving to Russia?"The video purportedly showed Lavrov criticising India's domestic affairs and its purchases of Russian oil.This comes as External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar met Lavrov on the sidelines of the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Atlanta, US, on October 31.Jaishankar shared a photograph of the meeting on X, saying, “Discussed the Ukraine conflict, Gulf situation and multilateral issues with FM Sergey Lavrov of Russia.”Addressing queries during the MEA's bi-weekly press briefing, spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said Jaishankar had held several bilateral meetings on the sidelines of the G20 gathering, including one with his Russian counterpart.The meeting between the two ministers covered the Ukraine conflict, the situation in the Gulf and wider multilateral issues.The interaction took place amid the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war and heightened tensions in West Asia, which have raised concerns over energy security, maritime trade routes and regional stability.India has continued to engage with Russia through high-level diplomatic meetings despite differences between Moscow and Western capitals over the Ukraine conflict. New Delhi has consistently maintained that dialogue and diplomacy are essential to resolving international disputes.At the G20 gathering, Jaishankar also emphasised the importance of diplomatic engagement over military action, maintaining that military solutions alone cannot resolve complex global challenges.
Article Summary: FIR against senior advocate Prashant Bhushan for sharing fake video of Russian minister criticising India. The video purportedly showed Lavrov criticise India's domestic affairs and its purchases of Russian oil. This comes as External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar met Lavrov on the sidelines of the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Atlanta.

Article Title: Rank-based merit list to replace percentile for NEET PG: Panel to SC
Article Text:
NMC gives in-principle approval to replace percentile-based NEET-PG and NEET-SS counselling with a rank-based system, under which only candidate ranks would be declared

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Medical postgraduate admissions could see a major change, with the National Medical Commission (NMC) giving in-principle approval to replace the existing percentile-based system with a rank-based system for NEET-PG and NEET-Super Speciality (SS) counselling.A 12-member expert committee constituted to review the NEET-PG admission and counselling process told Supreme Court in its report on Tuesday that the commission is working on a new regulation under which only ranks would be declared and percentile marks would no longer be specified.The proposal received in-principle approval at the NMC's meeting on Sept 23, according to a letter dated Oct 1, 2026, from the NMC secretary to the director general of health services (DGHS). The commission is yet to finalise the regulation.SC is examining various petitions challenging Centre's decision to drastically reduce the qualifying cut-off percentiles for NEET-PG 2025. Under revised criteria, the qualifying score for general category was reduced from 276 to 103, while that for SC/ST/OBC categories was brought down from 235 to minus 40.The report was filed after detailed deliberations and consideration of suggestions made by senior advocate Maninder Singh, who is assisting the Supreme Court as amicus curiae."NMC is in process of issuing new regulations, which are yet to be finalised wherein only rank-based system for NEET PG & SS counselling will be adopted; no percentile marks will be declared in results; only ranks will be given to candidates. A letter dated Oct 1 has been written by secretary, NMC to DGHS informing proposal for changing existing percentile-based system to a rank-based merit system for NEET-PG and NEET-SS which is under consideration by the Commission.The panel has accorded in-principle approval for proposed change with a view to address the issues arising from the existing system," the report said.On reduction of minimum qualification, the report said, "sanctity of NEET examinations should be maintained and minimum qualifying standards in postgraduate medical education is not diluted to the extent of permitting candidates with grossly inadequate or negative performance to become eligible for admission; the significance of competitive examinations should not be reduced to an administrative formality. "It also suggested that there should be no salary discrimination between residents of clinical and non-clinical branches and incentives should be given to doctors to work in rural areas.
Article Summary: National Medical Commission (NMC) gives in-principle approval to replace existing percentile-based system. NMC is in process of issuing new regulations, which are yet to be finalised. No percentile marks will be declared in results; only ranks will be given to candidates.

Article Title: Right to protest can't justify endless occupation of a site: SC
Article Text:
SC says no group or political outfit can occupy a protest site indefinitely, stresses need to balance the right to protest with traders’ and daily-wagers’ livelihoods

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Tuesday said no group, political party, NGO or civil society outfit could occupy a protest site indefinitely.A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said there were competing fundamental rights right to carry on trade and business and right to free speech and expression when senior advocate Mukul Rohatgi, appearing for traders, said the court must restrain all parties, NGO and civil society groups from holding protests in Delhi for the next two months to enable businesses to resume and to ensure that workers got their due.The court asked a traders’ association, which has sought Rs 1,000 crore in damages due to protests by CJP and opposition INDIA bloc during the festive season, to implead the protest organisers in the case for determination of compensation and how it is apportioned if it is awarded.Solicitor general Tushar Mehta said those who call for bandhs and agitations must bear responsibility towards compensating the loss caused to others. The bench asked Rohatgi to make the individuals, organisations and political parties responsible for protests and the resultant closure of shops parties in the petition.When senior advocates Menaka Guruswamy, Arundhati Katju, N Hariharan and others simultaneously argued that protests were part of the right to free speech and right of dissent in a democracy, the bench said, “The right to protest and right to trade and business are both constitutionally recognised fundamental rights.We are not talking about trade in the commercial sense.”CJI Kant said, “We are talking in terms of the source of livelihood of daily wagers, hawkers, rediwalas, sabziwalas – where will they go? Hence, a protest site must be identified which allows people to protest without hampering the livelihood of daily wagers.” The CJI emphasised that the right to protest was not an absolute right. “One set of protesters cannot occupy a designated protest site for all times to come... Everyone has a right to protest and they should be given a definite time period to protest...,” he added.Mehta said, “Calling for a protest without permission and asking people to march to Parliament cannot be permitted.” On denotification of Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site, Delhi Police commissioner Anurag Kumar said the decision was taken based on the recommendations of a committee constituted following the SC’s July 2018 order for regulating protests at Jantar Mantar.“The proximity of the new Parliament premises has further enhanced the significance of regulating activities in the surrounding areas, having regard to the security and uninterrupted functioning of a vital constitutional institution."
Article Summary: The court asked a traders’ association, which has sought Rs 1,000 crore in damages due to protests by CJP and opposition INDIA bloc during the festive season, to implead the protest organisers in the case. Solicitor general Tushar Mehta said those who call for bandhs and agitations must bear responsibility towards compensating the loss caused to others.

Article Title: 1.5-tonne Nasa space observatory set to crash on Earth today, possibility of debris parts falling in India
Article Text:
File photo: Nasa's 1.5-tonne Swift space observatory is set to re-enter Earth's atmosphere on Wednesday after 22 years, with some debris possibly falling over southern India.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: A 1.5-tonne space observatory of Nasa is heading back to Earth on Wednesday after working in space for 22 years and some parts of its debris could fall in southern India.Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory was launched in 2004 to explore the universe’s most powerful explosions called gamma-ray bursts. When launched, the spacecraft was a first-of-its-kind multiwavelength observatory designed to study the most powerful explosions in the cosmos using its three telescopes.“US Space Force predicted that the spacecraft will re-enter the atmosphere at approximately 3:30 a.m. EST, Nov. 4, with an uncertainty of 11 hours,” Nasa said on Monday.The US space agency expects most of the spacecraft to burn up as it travels through the atmosphere, but some components are expected to survive re-entry.Most surviving debris is expected to fall into the ocean. However, parts of India, Africa, Australia, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America could fall within the possible re-entry zone.The re-entry band spans between 20.6°N and 20.6°S latitude, which covers parts of southern India (including cities like Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Chennai, Bhubaneswar and Kochi).Isro has not said anything if it is tracking the descending space telescope.“If 70% of the Earth is ocean, 30% is land. So three out of 10 times it's on land, not ocean,” Brad Tucker, an astrophysicist at Australian National University, told ABC News.The Nasa observatory was originally designed for a two-year prime mission.However, the spacecraft was able to conduct science operations for more than two decades. Swift served as a multi-tool for exploring the universe, observing a wide range of light, rapidly pointing at short-lived outbursts, and sending alerts to other facilities to help coordinate follow-up observations.“The observatory has broadened our understanding of a wide variety of cosmic objects and events, from active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes and stars undergoing X-ray flares, to supernova explosions and comets and asteroids in our own solar system,” Nasa said.
Article Summary: Nasa's 1.5-tonne Swift space observatory is set to re-enter Earth's atmosphere on Wednesday after 22 years. The US space agency expects most of the spacecraft to burn up as it travels through the atmosphere, but some components are expected to survive re-entry. Most surviving debris is expected to fall into the ocean.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday flagged the alleged open sale of conventional and uncertified firecrackers in Delhi markets despite its recent order allowing only certified green crackers ahead of Diwali.A bench of Justices MM Sundresh and Prasanna B Varale referred to a media report published on Tuesday, which highlighted the availability of different varieties of firecrackers in several markets across the national capital, according to Bar and Bench.The bench asked Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati to look into the alleged violations."In today's report, there's a photograph, they say that notwithstanding yesterday's order, now everything is available in the (firecracker) shops. Please look into it," Justice Sundresh told Bhati.The judge also referred to the report's claims that licensed and unlicensed crackers, including those with and without QR codes, were being sold openly."They say that in the market every other cracker, licensed, unlicensed, QR code, or no QR code, everything is available. Please take a note of it," he said.Also read: SC on Diwali: Crackers on Nov 7-8 in 2 time slots, and keep it green On November 2, the Supreme Court allowed the sale of certified green firecrackers in Delhi-NCR from November 4 to 6 and their use on November 7 and 8, subject to restrictions.Firecrackers can be burst only between 6am and 7am and 8pm and 10pm on these two days. A complete ban will be restored from November 9.The court had clarified that only firecrackers certified by the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research-National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (CSIR-NEERI) and the Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation (PESO) could be manufactured and sold.It also restricted sales to designated locations and prohibited online sales. Each box must carry a product-specific QR code to verify its certification. The manufacture of firecracker strings, or laris, and crackers containing barium was also prohibited.
Article Summary: The Supreme Court on Tuesday flagged the alleged open sale of conventional and uncertified firecrackers in Delhi markets. NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday said no protest group can occupy a designated demonstration site indefinitely, observing that the right to protest must be balanced with the rights of other citizens. Hearing pleas filed by traders' associations over the impact of demonstrations in Delhi, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said designated protest venues must be made available to different groups for specific periods."You can't occupy a site for all times. Where farmers, journalists, etc. will go? Everyone has right to protest. Designated time must be given for designated period," CJI Surya Kant said, according to LiveLaw.The bench also said that orders granting permission for protests must clearly specify the reasons for allowing or refusing them. "You can't prevent other people, that I am doing protest now you can't," the CJI observed.The court was hearing pleas raising concerns over alleged police brutality, mass detentions, the closure of Metro stations and internet shutdowns during protests, besides the impact of demonstrations on businesses.A traders' counsel told the court that around 50 lakh people lived in areas surrounding the protest site and claimed that shops remained shut, with virtually nobody visiting Connaught Place. The court issued notices to the Centre and other authorities on a plea by the Kirana Committee Delhi seeking a halt to protests during the festive season.However, the bench said it could not adjudicate the traders' grievances unless all organisations involved in the protests were made parties to the proceedings. It asked the traders' associations to implead the organisers of the anti-CEC protests.The hearing comes weeks after the Centre de-notified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site, identifying Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground as alternative venues for demonstrations.
Article Summary: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said designated protest venues must be made available to different groups for specific periods. The bench also said that orders granting permission for protests must clearly specify the reasons for allowing or refusing them. The court issued notices to the Centre and other authorities on a plea by the Kirana Committee Delhi seeking a halt to protests.

Article Title: A first, Bangaluru company tests expandable space habitat tech in near-space mission
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: An experimental inflatable structure designed as a precursor to future orbital factories and expandable space habitats has completed its first high-altitude flight test, taking Bengaluru-based Akashalabdhi Space a step closer to demonstrating technologies for building infrastructure in space.The company flew “a 250-litre rigidizable inflatable structure” aboard a high-altitude balloon to approximately 30km, in a 25kg experimental mission conducted through the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research's (TIFR) National Balloon Facility in Hyderabad early on Tuesday (Nov 3).The flight carried two research payloads. The first, the Microbial Regolith Experiment (MRX), developed by Prof Aloke Kumar’s lab at IISc. It investigates microbial processes that could help consolidate regolith, the loose soil and rocky material covering the surfaces of the Moon and Mars, into construction materials.Biological methods of binding such material could eventually reduce the amount of building materials that future lunar and planetary missions would need to transport from Earth. The high-altitude flight provided an opportunity to expose the experiment to near-space conditions, with scientific assessment to follow after recovery.The balloon mission did not simulate sustained microgravity.Kumar said Tuesday’s test flight will give them enough data and confidence to prepare for an orbital test. TOI was the first to report about Kumar’s lab building bricks for Moon and Mars using Lunar and Martial soil simulants.The second was an experimental perovskite solar-cell payload from Switzerland-based Perovskia Solar. The experiment was intended to assess how photovoltaic technology responds to low atmospheric pressure, low temperatures and changing solar illumination.During the test, one outcome surprised Akashlabdhi. Its CEO Siddarth Jena told TOI: “The module, which was expected to sustain some damage during landing, absorbed the impact without the anticipated damage. The ability of the structure and its protective systems to withstand landing loads is important for future missions involving the recovery of experimental hardware and materials from space.”The mission was designed to test how an expandable structure behaves when deployed from a compactly packaged configuration, inflated and subsequently rigidised to retain its shape without depending continuously on internal pressure. Such structures could eventually provide larger working volumes for orbital manufacturing, commercial space stations, microgravity laboratories and habitation modules without requiring equally large launch-vehicle payload volumes.At the time of writing this copy, the company was still awaiting confirmation of two parameters before declaring all mission objectives achieved. These concern the performance of the solar-cell experiment and whether the parachute deployment achieved the targeted terminal velocity of 5 m/second.The balloon flight also offered an opportunity to assess the behaviour of onboard electronics, power systems, sensors, autonomous controls and telemetry under conditions of low atmospheric pressure and extreme cold.At approximately 30km, atmospheric pressure is only 1-2% of that at sea level, while temperatures can fall to around minus 45-50° Celsius. These conditions provide an intermediate testing environment between lab experiments and spaceflight, although they don’t replicate orbital vacuum, sustained microgravity or full radiation environment of space.The flight is part of its ANTARIKSHAB programme — TOI was the first to report about the programme — which aims to develop expandable infrastructure for future orbital manufacturing and habitation. The company is already looking beyond the balloon demonstration.Jena said the next major milestone is an orbital mission planned for March, using Skyroot’s Vikram-2 rocket. The proposed mission will carry a larger with the overall payload mass expected to be around 70kg. It will include two of the company’s material-development experiments to be conducted in microgravity and a data-centre payload.Tuesday’s flight provides the engineering data needed to refine the technology before it moves towards orbital qualification. It is an important intermediate step, rather than a demonstration of an operational space factory or an orbital re-entry system.
Article Summary: Akashalabdhi Space flew a 250-litre rigidizable inflatable structure aboard a high-altitude balloon to approximately 30km. The balloon flight also offered an opportunity to assess the behaviour of onboard electronics, power systems, sensors, autonomous controls and telemetry under conditions of low atmospheric pressure and extreme cold.

Article Title: One move, two gains: NHAI to desilt Bihar rivers and build roads with excavated material
Article Text:
Union road transport minister Nitin Gadkari and Bihar CM Samrat Choudhary at the signing of the 'Nadi Sanjivani' agreement.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: In a move aimed at tackling Bihar ’s perennial flooding problem while creating assets for road construction, road transport ministry and NHAI will undertake desilting of rivers and water bodies across the state at their own cost and use the excavated silt and sand for road construction.Under “Nadi Sanjivani” (river rejuvenation) framework, which was signed between road transport ministry and Bihar govt on Tuesday, the first-of-its-kind initiative, will serve two purposes -- highway agencies will carry out dredging and will get construction material for free, and it will improve water flow of rivers to reduce the risk of floods. Under this agreement, 243 lakh cubic metres of silt will be utilised in 16 ongoing national highway projects and another 835 lakh cubic metres is proposed for 27 future projects.Muddy water from Himalayas in Nepal flows into rivers passing through Bihar during rains, resulting in silt getting deposited in riverbeds, which causes floods every year. If the plan goes well, this problem would be addressed to a larger extent. “The silt that was the cause of floods until yesterday will now become the foundation for development,” Union road transport minister Nitin Gadkari said after signing of the agreement.He said this can be a template for other states to get construction materials from dredging of rivers and other water bodies. At present, highway builders get soil and other construction materials from far off places, which causes delay and pushes up construction cost.In his address, Bihar CM Samrat Choudhary highlighted the state’s vulnerability to recurring floods that cause losses to farmers, agricultural land, livelihoods and infrastructure. “Bihar doesn’t face destruction because of its water but because of water from neighbouring nations and other states. Seven prominent rivers from Nepal pass through Bihar and if it rains in Nepal, Bihar faces destruction... There was more than 32% less rain this year, but the highest flood level (HFL) changed in three major rivers.HFL of Ganga was maximum in the past 200 years,” he said.Choudhary said these were clear signs of deposit of silts in rivers and state govt quickly accepted the offer Gadkari made for desilting of rivers.Speaking at the event, NHAI chairman Santosh Yadav said the initiative is crucial considering that non-availability of soil can hold up embankment works and delay completion of highways. He said one-year of delay in under construction highway projects in Bihar is estimated to lead to around Rs 2,000 cr in civil cost escalation and around Rs 2,800 cr loss in toll remittance.
Article Summary: First-of-its-kind initiative will serve two purposes -- highway agencies will carry out dredging and will get construction material for free. Bihar CM Samrat Choudhary highlighted the state’s vulnerability to recurring floods that cause losses to farmers, agricultural land, livelihoods and infrastructure.

Article Title: India to oppose EU carbon tax at COP31, firms on fossil fuel use for its energy needs
Article Text:
File photo: Union environment minister Bhupender Yadav

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India will remain committed to protecting interests of its domestic industry against unilateral trade barriers such as European Union’s carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) and won’t support any move to phase out fossil fuels, keeping in view the country’s energy requirement for its development goals, said Union environment minister Bhupender Yadav on Tuesday. His remarks came as he prepares to lead a team of negotiators to the annual UN climate conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkiye, next week.Speaking about the country’s overall stand during the climate negotiation, Yadav said India will play a “constructive and bridge-building role”, seeking an outcome that moves from commitments to implementation and support.Turkish presidency of COP31, scheduled from Nov 9 to 20, has invited Prime Minister Narendra Modi for the leaders' summit of the UN climate conference. It is, however, not yet clear whether Modi will attend the Summit, scheduled for Nov 11-12.On COP31’s proposed “35-by-35” electrification goal that aims to raise electricity’s share of global final energy demand from about 23% today to 35% by 2035, the minister said India will underline that voluntary initiatives under Presidency Action Agenda should remain separate from negotiations and that uniform global targets must respect national circumstances.Though the minister preferred not to comment on the presidency’s global electrification goal, his emphasis on respecting “national circumstances” clearly indicates that India would weigh all options before committing to any such global target which will not be part of the formal negotiation process.As far as CBAM, which entered its operational regime on Jan 1, is concerned, India opposed the proposal from the time it was conceived, arguing that such a unilateral move placed an additional burden on businesses in developing economies due to embedded emissions in their products.CBAM is a tool to put a price, through imposing a border tax, on carbon-intensive goods, like iron and steel, aluminium and cement, that are entering the 27 EU nations.Even all the BRICS nations, including China, Russia, South Africa, Brazil and others, formally opposed it and any other such trade barriers, calling them “unilateral, punitive, discriminatory and protectionist measures”, when they assembled here for the annual summit under India’s chairship in Sept.Reaffirming that India stands committed to make positive contributions to global efforts to achieve objectives of climate convention and goals of Paris Agreement, Yadav said climate finance will be a key priority, with India seeking a COP31 decision to commence the Climate Finance Work Programme.He also emphasised that finance is an obligation of developed countries under the Paris Agreement and must be "predictable, largely public and concessional", and should not add to the debt burden.
Article Summary: India won't support any move to phase out fossil fuels, says Union environment minister Bhupender Yadav. His remarks came as he prepares to lead a team of negotiators to UN climate conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkiye, next week.

Article Title: Bhutan's glacial lake outburst exposes growing disaster threat across the Himalayas
Article Text:
One flood, another potential disaster

Melting glaciers raise Himalayan disaster risks

A Bhutan study reveals the scale of the threat

Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences

Hydropower infrastructure faces a major risk

India faces risks beyond its Himalayan states

Early-warning systems remain critical to saving lives

A regional threat needs a regional response

Bhutan's glacial lake outburst has exposed a growing threat facing the Himalaya, where retreating glaciers, expanding glacial lakes and increasingly unstable mountain terrain are raising the risk of sudden, cascading disasters.The October 29 outburst from Sintaphu Lake in the country's Gasa district sent a torrent of water and debris downstream, damaging roads and bridges, disrupting connectivity to remote settlements and triggering flood alerts in parts of India's West Bengal and Assam.The situation took a more concerning turn when debris from the flood obstructed a downstream river channel, creating a temporary lake at Taktsemakhang and raising fears of a possible secondary flood.Although no casualties were reported, the incident has brought the vulnerability of Himalayan communities and critical infrastructure into sharp focus. Beyond the immediate damage, it has raised a larger question: are countries sharing Himalayan river systems prepared for the cascading disasters that a rapidly changing mountain environment could trigger?The danger did not end with the initial outburst. As the floodwaters travelled downstream, they carried large quantities of rocks, soil and sediment, which accumulated at the confluence of Sintaphu Chhu and Lungu Chhu, also known as Gangchen Tag Chhu.The resulting blockage caused water to accumulate at Taktsemakhang in Bhutan's Gasa district, creating a temporary lake and raising concerns about another possible flood.The formation of such temporary lakes is a known secondary hazard associated with glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs). Powerful floodwaters can erode river valleys and deposit large volumes of debris downstream, creating natural barriers that obstruct river channels. If these blockages weaken or collapse, the accumulated water can be released suddenly, triggering another potentially devastating flood.As of November 2, the temporary lake was reported to be stable, with no noticeable rise in water levels and its outflow remaining constant. Bhutanese authorities were monitoring the site, while controlled explosions were being considered to facilitate the drainage of accumulated water.However, a subsequent report by Bhutan Broadcasting Service on November 3 said a substantial volume of water remained in the upper lake. The possibility of another outburst had not been ruled out, although authorities were yet to verify the situation through a physical inspection. The precise trigger of the October 29 outburst also remained unconfirmed.The Bhutan outburst is part of a wider environmental shift unfolding across the Hindu Kush Himalaya, where rising temperatures are accelerating glacier loss and transforming the region's high-altitude landscape.As glaciers retreat, meltwater collects in depressions left behind by the ice, forming new glacial lakes or causing existing ones to expand. Many of these lakes are held back by natural barriers of loose rocks, soil and glacial debris, known as moraines. These barriers are vulnerable to erosion, slope instability and the impact of avalanches or landslides entering the lake. A breach can release enormous volumes of water downstream, triggering a GLOF.The scale of this transformation is reflected in a 2026 assessment by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD). It found that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya lost around 12 percent of their total area and 9 percent of their estimated ice reserves between 1990 and 2020. The rate of ice loss doubled after 2000.Speaking to TOI, Dr Rijan Bhakta Kayastha, visiting senior professor at the Department of Environmental Science, Kathmandu University, said rising temperatures at higher elevations were accelerating glacier melt and destabilising mountain slopes."Due to higher air temperature at higher elevation in recent years, old permafrost are melting and ground or slopes are destabilized. In such cases, a huge slope may collapse into a lake and GLOF can initiate," he said.He added, "Due to high ice melting supra-glacier ponds/lakes may drain water through englacial channels releasing a huge amount of water causing a devastating flood in the downstream."Referring to Bhutan's October 29 outburst, Kayastha said, "The cause of the GLOF has not been identified yet, but high ice melting due to higher air temperature and sudden release of huge meltwater from the mother glacier cannot be ruled out."The potential scale of the danger is highlighted in a study published in the journalin March 2026. Researchers modelled possible glacial lake outburst floods from 278 lakes in Bhutan, each covering more than 0.05 square kilometres and located within one kilometre of a glacier.The study found that potential GLOFs could expose 11,322 people, 2,613 buildings, 270 kilometres of roads, 402 bridges and 19 square kilometres of farmland to flooding. Four hydropower dams were also identified within potential impact zones.The researchers classified Thorthormi Tsho as a very-high-hazard lake and identified five others as high hazard. Three of these — Phudung Tsho, lake251 and Wonney Tsho — had not been classified as high hazard in earlier assessments.The study also highlighted significant gaps in Bhutan's early-warning network. Of the 278 lakes assessed, only 51 were covered by the existing monitoring system. This included Thorthormi Tsho and just two of the five high-hazard lakes, leaving three newly identified high-hazard lakes outside the monitoring network.The findings are based on computer simulations of hypothetical flood scenarios, not predictions that these lakes will burst. Nevertheless, they underline why assessing a lake's danger must go beyond its size or the likelihood of a breach. The communities and infrastructure exposed downstream are equally important considerations.The threat extends beyond villages, roads and bridges. Bhutan's economy is heavily dependent on hydropower, with major power projects located along rivers fed by glaciers in the northern mountains.A severe GLOF could send enormous volumes of water, rocks and sediment downstream, threatening dams, power stations, transmission links and other critical facilities. Damage to these assets could disrupt electricity generation and affect power exports to India.The 2026 study identified four hydropower dams within potential GLOF impact zones. It also highlighted the exposure of roads, bridges and settlements along glacier-fed river valleys, underlining how a single outburst could affect multiple parts of the infrastructure network.For Bhutan, where hydropower is a major source of export revenue, the consequences could extend well beyond the immediate impact of floodwaters on dams. Damage to access roads, transmission infrastructure and other connected facilities could also disrupt the functioning of power projects.Dr Rijan Bhakta Kayastha stressed the need for hydropower developers to assess risks across entire river basins before undertaking projects."Hydropower developers should study the whole river basin before they initiate their project, and precautional measures should be taken for huge glacial floods," he said.The challenge, therefore, is not simply to protect individual dams. It is also to ensure that warnings reach downstream communities in time, access roads remain functional and emergency plans account for damage across interconnected infrastructure.The threat posed by glacial lake outburst floods does not stop at national borders. Rivers originating in the Bhutan Himalaya flow into India, carrying the potential impact of a sudden outburst far downstream.The October 29 incident demonstrated this vulnerability. The Central Water Commission (CWC) warned that floodwaters moving through the Punatsangchhu river system, known as the Sankosh in India, could reach the border within six to eight hours. Alipurduar in West Bengal and Dhubri in Assam were identified as areas potentially at risk.The warning prompted evacuations in vulnerable parts of north Bengal, while authorities in Assam monitored the situation along the Sankosh. Around 12,000 people were moved to safer locations in Alipurduar district. Although the immediate threat later eased, the episode showed how a disaster originating in Bhutan could put communities across the border at risk within hours.India has already experienced the destructive consequences of such events. In October 2023, the breach of South Lhonak Lake in Sikkim triggered a devastating flood in the Teesta river, causing the collapse of the Teesta-III hydropower dam and extensive damage downstream. The Central Water Commission documented the event as a major GLOF-related flood.Together, the Bhutan and Sikkim incidents underline the vulnerability of communities and infrastructure along Himalayan river systems. They also demonstrate why disaster preparedness cannot be confined to the country in which a glacial lake is located.The growing threat of GLOFs has placed early-warning systems and evacuation preparedness at the centre of disaster management across the Himalaya.Monitoring glacial lakes can help authorities identify potential dangers, but surveillance alone is not enough. Reliable forecasting, rapid communication and clearly defined evacuation plans are equally critical to ensuring warnings reach vulnerable communities before floodwaters arrive.Bhutan's early-warning network in the Punatsangchhu basin became operational in the Pho Chhu sub-basin in 2011 and was expanded to the Mochhu sub-basin in 2013. However, the 2026 Bhutan study's finding that only 51 of the 278 lakes assessed were covered by the existing monitoring network highlights the limitations of current surveillance.Bhutan is now working to strengthen its warning infrastructure. In September 2026, Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay said the existing systems were functioning but had become old and needed improvement. The government was developing a proposal to expand early-warning coverage across the country's major river basins. A concept note worth US$22 million had been approved by the Green Climate Fund in June 2026, with a full proposal being developed in collaboration with the United Nations Environment Programme.India, meanwhile, has begun reviewing preparedness across its Himalayan states. In September 2026, Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan chaired a meeting with officials from five Himalayan states and Union territories to assess glacial lake monitoring, warning mechanisms, evacuation plans and disaster-response arrangements.Dr Rijan Bhakta Kayastha said Himalayan countries were not adequately prepared for increasingly unpredictable glacial floods."Most of the Himalayan nations are not well prepared for such uncertain glacial floods. All are concentrating on bigger glacial lakes in the past but now from the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli and Budhigandaki Glacial disasters, we need to monitor and watch carefully all high elevation glaciers and hanging glaciers, too," he said.He called for a much wider monitoring network, saying, "Therefore, we need to monitor all glaciers at high elevation, hanging glaciers, large snow fields, glacial lakes, permafrost zones and rivers flowing from glacierized river basins using satellite data, automatic weather stations, water level sensors, field cameras and seismic sensors for robust early warning system."The Bhutan outburst has shown how quickly a disaster in the high mountains can cross borders, disrupt critical infrastructure and threaten communities far downstream. With glaciers retreating and glacial lakes expanding across the Hindu Kush Himalaya, the danger is no longer confined to isolated mountain valleys.For India, Bhutan and other countries sharing Himalayan river systems, the priority must be stronger cross-border coordination, regular monitoring of vulnerable lakes, reliable early-warning networks and evacuation plans that account for cascading hazards.Hydropower projects and other critical infrastructure must also be assessed against the changing risks posed by glacial floods.The challenge is not simply to prevent every glacial lake from bursting, an outcome that may not be possible. It is to ensure that when an outburst occurs, authorities have enough time, information and coordination to limit its impact. As the Himalayan landscape continues to change, preparedness is no longer just a national responsibility. It is a regional necessity.
Article Summary: The October 29 outburst from Sintaphu Lake in Bhutan sent a torrent of water and debris downstream, damaging roads and bridges. The situation took a more concerning turn when debris from the flood obstructed a downstream river channel, creating a temporary lake. The formation of such temporary lakes is a known secondary hazard associated with glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs)

Article Title: 'Incompatible with secular character': Centre tells Delhi HC mosque inside Krishi Bhawan must be demolished
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Centre on Tuesday informed the Delhi high court that it is planning to remove a mosque situated within the Krishi Bhawan complex to facilitate the redevelopment and reconstruction of the Common Central Secretariat under the Central Vista project.In a status report filed through the Land and Development Office, the Centre also submitted that Krishi Bhawan and the Central Secretariat complex are secular public premises dedicated exclusively to administrative functions. It said the establishment or retention of a permanent religious structure within a central government office complex would be incompatible with the secular character of government property.The Centre maintained that Qadeemi Masjid stands on government-owned land and that its caretaking committee was granted only permissive possession of the premises under an agreement executed on November 8, 1940.The government also claimed that the agreement did not confer any ownership rights, title or interest in the property upon the managing committee.The agreement contained a provision empowering government authorities to take back possession of the property in the event of any breach or default in complying with its terms and conditions.The Centre has relied on an agreement dated November 8, 1940, executed between the then government, as the owner of the property, and the secretary of the managing committee of Jama Masjid.Under the agreement, the government had granted permissive possession of the premises to the committee exclusively for use as a mosque.The agreement also imposed several restrictions on the use and modification of the property, prohibiting the managing committee from making alterations, undertaking repairs to the existing buildings, constructing graves or raising any new structure, even temporarily, without obtaining prior written approval from the government.Mosque required to be removed for execution of Central Vista projectThe Centre said the removal of the structure was necessary as the Central Vista Redevelopment Master Plan provides for the redevelopment and reconstruction of Common Central Secretariat Buildings 4 and 5 at Plot No. 120, covering the existing sites of Shastri Bhawan and Krishi Bhawan.According to the status report, the proposed project is aimed at modernising infrastructure considered essential for the country's governance and administrative functioning. The government has asserted that the mosque presently stands within the identified project site and is required to be removed for the execution of the proposed construction.Describing the construction of CCS Buildings 4 and 5 as a public project of paramount national importance, the Centre also argued that retaining the mosque or reserving any portion of the project site for the religious structure would be inconsistent with the redevelopment master plan.The L&DO has further argued that public land situated in a central administrative zone cannot be permanently reserved for a religious structure.Based on these submissions, the Centre has maintained that the managing committee cannot claim a right to compel the government to allot or earmark a separate portion of land for the mosque within the Krishi Bhawan compound or the Central Secretariat complex.The government has also disputed any violation of the fundamental right to freedom of religion guaranteed under Article 25 of the Constitution.It has submitted that the constitutional provision does not confer a right to insist on worship at a particular place on government land held under a permissive arrangement.The government's response comes in reply to a petition filed by Qadeemi Masjid through its caretaking committee, challenging the proposed action concerning the religious structure.The petition further states that the Delhi Waqf Board notified the property as Waqf property in 1970 and recorded its antiquity.The petitioners claimed that even after Krishi Bhawan, Shastri Bhawan and surrounding government offices were constructed in the 1950s and 1960s, the mosque continued to exist and was used by Muslim employees of the offices for offering prayers.The petitioners acknowledged that the land underneath the mosque is government property but expressed apprehension over the ongoing redevelopment, which involves dismantling the existing complex.They maintained that they have no objection to the Central Vista redevelopment project and are not seeking a suspension or delay in the construction of the Common Central Secretariat buildings.
Article Summary: The Centre is planning to remove a mosque situated within the Krishi Bhawan complex to facilitate the redevelopment of the Common Central Secretariat under the Central Vista project. The Centre said the establishment or retention of a permanent religious structure within a central government office complex would be incompatible with the secular character of government property.

Article Title: At Anant Ambani’s Vantara, global zoos turn to shared data to protect wildlife
Article Text:
Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe that technology plays a crucial role in wildlife conservation? Yes No 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

The EARAZA Annual Conference 2026 concluded at Vantara in Jamnagar, bringing together wildlife professionals, veterinarians, scientists and conservation leaders from 98 institutions across 30 countries, along with representatives of 29 Indian zoological institutions.Held under the theme “Strengthening Global Partnerships for Wildlife Conservation”, the four-day conference focused on cross-border conservation programmes, animal welfare, wildlife medicine, technology, crisis response and public engagement.The conference opened on October 26 with a performance by three-time Grammy Award-winning composer and environmentalist Ricky Kej. The inauguration was followed by a traditional lamp-lighting ceremony attended by Vivaan Karani, CEO, Vantara; Svetlana Akulova, president, EARAZA; Prof Raman Sukumar of the Indian Institute of Science; Dr V Clement Ben, member secretary, Central Zoo Authority; and Dr Brij Kishor Gupta, director, Gujarat Zoological Research and Rescue Centre.The Indian Zoo Yearbook, Volume 11, 2026, was also released during the opening ceremony.As host, Vantara announced that the ANTZ Software Platform would be offered free of cost to all EARAZA members for one year. ANTZ is a zoological management platform with an Open Data Exchange that enables participating institutions to share information across the network.The announcement aligned with one of the conference's key themes: the need for conservation knowledge and data to move more easily between institutions and across national borders. Akulova spoke about the importance of creating global data infrastructure for biodiversity conservation, allowing information generated by one institution to inform decisions elsewhere.The sessions covered coordinated conservation programmes for the Amur tiger, Oriental stork, Blakiston’s eagle-owl and great bustard. Discussions also examined the conservation breeding of Boiga snakes, the reintroduction of the long-eared hedgehog, the conservation of the Indian wild ass and the ex-situ conservation of the Amur tiger.The second day focused on coexistence, urban biodiversity and public engagement. Sessions examined snake conservation and snakebite prevention, biodiversity conservation in million-plus cities and the role of citizen science.A panel on “Animal Welfare: From Inputs to Measurable Outcomes”, moderated by Karani, discussed how care practices can be assessed through measurable outcomes for individual animals. Other sessions addressed the visitor experience at zoological institutions, conservation education and the role of mass media. Wildlife biologist and television presenter Forrest Galante spoke about taking conservation conversations to wider audiences.Delegates also discussed crisis management in wildlife-care facilities and disaster response in the wild. Presentations covered polar bear rescue, wildlife disease diagnostics, animal nutrition and the work of zoological institutions in Russia. Padma Shri awardee Dr K K Sarma, known for his work with elephants, shared field perspectives on human-wildlife conflict.The conference also included interactive formats such as “The Elephant in the Room”, where delegates reflected on difficult questions facing the zoological sector, and the Solution Station, which invited professionals to bring real challenges in wildlife care and conservation for expert guidance.Technology and research took centre stage on the third day. Vantara presented tools developed under the ANTZ platform, including Vespr, an edge-AI bioacoustic monitor that identifies species on the device; Smart Egg Analysis, which helps teams measure and monitor eggs; and an NFC-enabled system for digitally recording animal-care rounds.Scientific presentations by Vantara experts covered non-invasive population genomics of Asiatic lions, paraveterinary training, avian rewilding, the use of artificial intelligence to understand animals and efforts to bridge ex-situ and in-situ conservation.Alongside the sessions, the conference featured an exhibition with 13 exhibitors from seven countries. The displays included veterinary technologies, wildlife diagnostics, genomics, automated microscopy, assisted reproduction systems, avian incubation equipment and remote drug-delivery solutions. Vantara’s host pavilions also featured innovations in wildlife care, nutrition, architecture and technology, along with a virtual reality experience.The final day focused on science-based care for rescued Asian elephants, animal nutrition in rescue and rewilding, habitat change, cryopreservation, triage and parasite surveillance. Dr Manilal Valliyate, chief communication officer at Vantara, moderated a panel on veterinary capacity-building.The conference concluded with a gala dinner and closing ceremony, where Lifetime Achievement Awards were presented to six leaders from India and abroad: Svetlana Akulova, René Franěk, Azer Huseynov, S C Sharma, Dr D N Singh and Dr B S Bonal.The EARAZA flag was then handed over to China, host of the 2027 conference. The event concluded with a vote of thanks by Dr Brij Kishor Gupta.
Article Summary: The EARAZA Annual Conference 2026 concluded at Vantara in Jamnagar. It brought together wildlife professionals, veterinarians, scientists and conservation leaders from 98 institutions across 30 countries. Four-day conference focused on cross-border conservation programmes, animal welfare, wildlife medicine, technology, crisis response and public engagement.

Article Title: NHAI to use desilted river material for road projects in Bihar, says transport minister Gadkari
Article Text:
The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) has embarked on an innovative project to leverage materials from Bihar's rivers for highway development

The national highways authority of India (NHAI) will use sand and other materials excavated from rivers and water bodies in Bihar for highway construction, union road transport minister Nitin Gadkari said after the Bihar government and the road transport ministry signed an MoU.Nitin Gadkari said the initiative would also help mitigate flooding in the state.The Bihar chief minister said the state faces floods not only due to its own water but also because of water flowing in from other regions, including Nepal. He noted that the highest flood levels (HFL) had risen in three rivers despite Bihar receiving less rainfall this year.Desilting rivers and water bodies could help reduce the impact of floods, the chief minister said, adding that desilting the Ganga and reclaiming land along its banks could create space for one lakh Ganga-facing homes.
Article Summary: National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) will use sand and other materials excavated from rivers and water bodies in Bihar for highway construction. Nitin Gadkari said the initiative would also help mitigate flooding in the state. Desilting the Ganga and reclaiming land along its banks could create space for one lakh Ganga-facing homes.

Article Title: 'Rs 14,000cr loss last month': Delhi traders seek protest-free Delhi till November 11
Article Text:
The organisation has argued that repeated disruptions have affected markets

NEW DELHI: Chamber of Trade and Industry (CTI) on Tuesday wrote to Delhi Police Commissioner, seeking a ban on rallies, sit-ins, protests and marches across the national capital until November 11. The trade body cited significant business losses caused by demonstrations over the past month.In its letter, the traders' body urged police not to grant permission for such events, particularly in areas including Connaught Place, Jantar Mantar, Ramlila Maidan, India Gate, Rajghat, Delhi Gate, Central Delhi and Old Delhi. The request comes amid concerns over disruptions to commercial activity during the festive season.According to CTI estimates, protests and demonstrations held over the past month have resulted in losses amounting to Rs 14,000 crore for Delhi's trading community. The organisation has argued that repeated disruptions have affected markets, restricted customer movement and hit business activity across several parts of the city.The demand comes days after the INDIA bloc's rally at Ramlila Maidan triggered a political row over its impact on traders.CTI chairman Brijesh Goyal had earlier estimated that the event alone caused losses of Rs 10,000-11,000 crore, claiming that around 2.5 lakh shops out of nearly three lakh in 20-25 major markets near the venue remained closed.The Congress, however, disputed these claims. Senior party leader Jairam Ramesh alleged that the BJP had spread a false narrative about business losses to discredit the rally, claiming that traders had instead benefited from the arrival of visitors from across the country.Leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi had also accused the BJP of "forcibly shutting down" shops in Connaught Place ahead of the rally, saying participants had been encouraged to support local businesses but found several establishments closed.Union home minister Amit Shah had earlier criticised the opposition for holding the rally ahead of Diwali despite traders' requests to postpone it, citing concerns over losses during the crucial festive shopping period.
Article Summary: Chamber of Trade and Industry (CTI) wrote to Delhi Police Commissioner, seeking a ban on rallies, sit-ins, protests and marches across the national capital until November 11. The trade body cited significant business losses caused by demonstrations over the past month. The request comes amid concerns over disruptions to commercial activity during the festive season.

Article Title: Watch: Tamil Nadu CM Vijay launches one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns
Article Text:
Vijay presented 22-carat, one-gram gold rings to 25 newborns. (PTI)

Who is eligible for the gold ring?

Scheme draws on Tamil tradition

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Monday rolled out the state government’s one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns in Madurai. He also held some of the newborns and presented the rings to beneficiaries during the launch programme.Under the scheme, eligible babies born in government hospitals and government primary health centres will receive a 22-carat, one-gram gold ring.The initiative, named the Maternal Uncle Gold Ring Scheme (Thaaimaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam), has an annual allocation of Rs 755.83 crore.It is aimed at celebrating motherhood, promoting maternal and child health and encouraging institutional deliveries by increasing public confidence in government healthcare facilities.The scheme will cover babies born on or after June 22, 2026, to mothers who are permanent residents of Tamil Nadu and have delivered at government healthcare institutions.Mothers must be registered under the Pregnancy and Infant Cohort Monitoring and Evaluation (PICME) system and have a Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) ID. They will also have to provide an e-KYC-verified Aadhaar card along with one of the prescribed identity or residence documents.These include ration cards, voter identity cards, Labour Welfare Board identity cards, Department of Posts address cards and nativity certificates.The state government has already procured 1.28 lakh one-gram gold rings for the initial rollout. Each ring will have a unique serial number and will be packed in tamper-proof packaging.From Monday, babies born in government hospitals will receive the rings at the time of discharge, according to the state government.To clear the backlog of eligible babies born between June 22 and Monday, the government will distribute the rings through 107 hubs across Tamil Nadu.Distribution will begin at the rate of 100 babies per day at each hub. At designated centres, 25 beneficiaries will be accommodated in the morning and another 25 in the afternoon to avoid overcrowding, PTI reported.Village Health Nurses will distribute invitations informing beneficiaries of their allotted date and time. Beneficiaries have been asked to visit the designated centres only at the time mentioned in their invitations.The district administration has also made transportation arrangements for beneficiaries from their respective areas. Vijay had announced the scheme ahead of the April 23 Assembly election as a symbolic gift to newborns, drawing on the Tamil tradition of ‘Thaimaaman Seer’. The scheme has retrospective effect from June 22, Vijay’s birthday.A government order issued on June 23 described the initiative as a token celebrating the birth of a child, motherhood and the cultural tradition of ‘Thaimaaman’.According to ANI, Tamil Nadu minister Arun Raj explained the cultural significance of the initiative saying, "A maternal uncle is someone who is among the first to rush in when a child is born, sharing in his sister’s happiness as his own. He assures her that he will always stand by her and her child, offering love, support and a sense of security.""Today, the Tamil Nadu Government, under the leadership of our brother, Mr. Vijay, is embracing this sacred bond of the maternal uncle and, as a gesture of that affection, is set to provide a one-gram gold ring to every child born in government hospitals. When the scheme was announced and the question arose as to where it should be launched, the place chosen by our Chief Minister was Madurai. This is the sacred soil of Madurai, blessed with the compassion and grace of Mother Meenakshi," he added.Tamil Nadu records around 7.8 lakh deliveries annually, with institutional deliveries accounting for 99.9% of births, according to NFHS-6. Government health facilities account for nearly 4.2 lakh deliveries, or around 53% of the total.According to the state government, the average out-of-pocket expenditure for a delivery at a government hospital is Rs 1,364, compared with Rs 63,473 at a private hospital.The government said the scheme is intended to encourage safe institutional deliveries, strengthen maternal and child welfare and increase public trust in government healthcare services.The Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation will procure the gold rings based on annual requirements, while a project and programme management unit will oversee implementation and monitoring.
Article Summary: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Monday rolled out the state government’s one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns in Madurai. The scheme will cover babies born on or after June 22, 2026, to mothers who are permanent residents of Tamil Nadu and have delivered at government healthcare institutions. Vijay had announced the scheme ahead of the April 23 Assembly election.

Article Title: Delhi landfill garbage mountains shrinking, 100 acres reclaimed in 18 months: CM Rekha Gupta
Article Text:
Delhi CM Rekha Gupta poses for a group picture during an on-site inspection of waste disposal operations near Okhla, in New Delhi

Government targets legacy and fresh waste

New processing plants at three sites

Focus on pollution and waste management

NEW DELHI: Delhi chief minister Rekha Gupta on Saturday said the garbage mountains at the city's landfill sites were steadily shrinking as she reviewed waste disposal work at Okhla and laid the foundation stone for new waste processing facilities at Okhla, Ghazipur and Singhola.Gupta said the Delhi government had reclaimed 100 acres of land across the city's three landfill sites over the past one-and-a-half years, with a large portion of the cleared area also being turned green.She said almost all legacy waste at Okhla that existed before January 2025 had been processed."Today, at Okhla, we have processed almost all the legacy waste that was there before January 2025," Gupta said.Gupta said the government was working on two fronts: clearing the existing garbage mountains while ensuring that fresh waste generated every day did not accumulate into new landfill sites.According to news agency ANI, she said around 3,000-4,000 metric tonnes of fresh waste reaches the sites daily and is being processed round the clock."The garbage currently piled up here is essentially fresh waste generated after January 2025, and that too is being processed round the clock. So, we are fighting on two fronts: one is eliminating waste, and the other is ensuring that the 3,000 to 4,000 metric tons of fresh waste arriving daily is processed immediately, so that new garbage mountains are not formed for future generations," Gupta said.She said the government was working to reduce the existing garbage mountains to zero."People are seeing that the garbage mountains are continuously shrinking and soon a time will come when they will become zero," Gupta said.Gupta also said she had taken what she described as her "last selfie" with the garbage mountain at Okhla."Today I have taken my last selfie with the garbage mountain; after this I have taken a pledge that this garbage mountain will end soon," she said.Taking a jibe at the Opposition, Gupta added, "I had said - garbage mountain, you will have to go; the opposition mocked. Today I will say the garbage mountain is going; now only its back remains."During the programme at the Okhla SLF site, Gupta laid the foundation stone for fresh waste processing plants at Okhla, Ghazipur and Singhola, as well as a biogas facility at Ghazipur. She also inaugurated the M&CW Centre at Kotla Mubarakpur through virtual mode from Okhla.The Okhla plant will be built at a cost of Rs 103 crore and will have a processing capacity of 1,400 metric tonnes per day.The Singhola facility will cost Rs 42 crore and have a capacity of 800 metric tonnes per day, while the Ghazipur plant will have a processing capacity of 700 metric tonnes per day.The facilities are intended to process fresh waste as well as construction and demolition waste. Gupta said the new units would also produce biogas, green energy and manure."Waste should not remain waste; Delhi should use it as wealth," she said, adding that new technologies were being introduced for waste segregation and processing.She said waste and cattle dung would be used to produce biogas and manure as part of efforts to build a technology-driven waste management system.Gupta said the government was taking up several measures to address pollution, including work on landfill waste, cleaning the Yamuna, dust mitigation, plantation, road infrastructure and waste management."Our government is tackling pollution from a 360-degree perspective to ensure it gradually decreases. We are working on every aspect, be it addressing the mountains of garbage, cleaning the Yamuna, improving road infrastructure, or managing waste, to ensure the people of Delhi enjoy better air quality. Our resolve and policies are absolutely clear, and we are working 24x7 in the public interest," she said.The chief minister also reviewed the progress of waste disposal work with officials and directed them to accelerate the work according to the stipulated timeline.She said the garbage mountains at Bhalswa, Ghazipur and Okhla had caused inconvenience to people travelling through these areas and said the government was continuing efforts to eliminate them.
Article Summary: Gupta said the Delhi government had reclaimed 100 acres of land across the city's three landfill sites over the past one-and-a-half years. She said almost all legacy waste at Okhla that existed before January 2025 had been processed. Gupta said the new units would also produce biogas, green energy and manure.

Article Title: India-US trade talks hit ‘plateau’: Sitharaman says further give-and-take ‘very, very difficult’
Article Text:
Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman

India stresses strategic autonomy in trade negotiations

India-EU pact opens market access

India and US have reached a “plateau” in negotiations over their bilateral trade agreement, with further concessions from either side likely to be "very very difficult", finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Monday. Speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi, she said that while negotiations are still underway, any progress from here would depend on whether there was limited room for compromise on either side.“The agreement negotiations are still ongoing, although we'd like to believe that both the sides have reached a plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult. But maybe if there are rooms to operate from, both sides would do it,” Sitharaman said.She said the agreement was still being “hard and very rigorously negotiated” and that India has a trade surplus with the US. “But what is the predominant feature of the trade relations between India and the US? The trade balance is very much in our favor.”Sitharaman said that the US would naturally want to reduce this trade imbalance and address what it sees as losses built up over the years.She also said that the way countries negotiate trade deals was changing, with governments now looking beyond traditional negotiations to address trade imbalances.“Negotiation used to be the only platform through which countries could highlight the discrepancies, highlight the lop-sidedness and say, would we want to correct this?” she said.“Tariff was an instrument of negotiation, and tariff had a certain framework within which you will apply it. Today framework is there, tariffs are going,” she said, while stressing that countries still need to negotiate and find “some give and take”.Sitharaman was also asked about maintaining strategic autonomy while negotiating bilateral trade agreements with European countries, including in the context of India procuring Russian oil."There is no Lindsay Graham Bill in Europe...," she said.On the broader question of how bilateral trade agreements can protect a country's interests in an era of multilateralism, Sitharaman said countries were increasingly choosing bilateral partnerships where they saw greater benefit.“Countries choose where multilateralism would benefit them, and there are some unique bilaterals which countries choose to have. The balance is somewhat tilted in favour of the bilateral rather than the multilateral,” she said.She said countries were now increasingly looking for new trade partners and strengthening those relationships through agreements.“Countries are now rapidly catching up with — I would put the EU-India also in a bilateral mode -because it's one in the name of union, but of course within them they have. So, bilaterals today are catching up far more than even initiating or beginning a multilateral. It's not deliberate, but in a way, if you don't do it, you're not moving forward. Countries will have to choose new partners for their trade and strengthen the tie through an agreement. And therefore, newer partnerships are being searched for, and they are tied up bilaterally.”FM Sitharaman cited the India-EU trade agreement as a major example of India's approach to negotiating trade pacts while protecting domestic interests.She said India had opened 92.5 per cent of its tariff lines and around 97 per cent of tariff value under the agreement. The EU, meanwhile, had opened 99 per cent in value terms and possibly 97 per cent of tariff lines.According to Sitharaman, greater access to the European market could support employment in labour-intensive sectors, including footwear, textiles, toys and processed products. Many of these sectors are linked to micro and small enterprises.“Those are all in the micro and small medium industry segment, which are labor-intensive,” Sitharaman said, adding that greater access to the European market could generate “more exports, more jobs”.Sitharaman said bilateral trade agreements were becoming increasingly important as multilateral institutions have weakened.“Multilateralism is not going to go away. But multilateralism has weakened,” she said.She also stressed that multilateralism should continue even as countries increasingly pursue bilateral agreements.“Multilateralism is not going to go away and multilateralism shouldn't go away,” Sitharaman said.The Munich Leaders Meeting, being held in the National Capital, provides a platform for about 100 senior decision-makers and experts to discuss opportunities for stronger cooperation among emerging and middle powers amid profound geopolitical change. Discussions include geoeconomic developments, trade and connectivity, maritime security, defence cooperation and other key international challenges.
Article Summary: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman says India and US have reached a 'plateau' in negotiations over their bilateral trade agreement. She said any progress from here would depend on whether there was limited room for compromise on either side. She also said the way countries negotiate trade deals was changing, with governments now looking beyond traditional negotiations to address trade imbalances.

Article Title: Jio IPO sees bumper demand: India's largest public issue fully subscribed in just 100 minutes of opening
Article Text:
The IPO is open to retail investors, employees and eligible Reliance shareholders.

Jio IPO

Jio IPO: Jio Platforms' $3.2 billion initial public offering (IPO) was fully subscribed within less than two hours of bidding opening on Wednesday, as investors rushed to participate in India's biggest-ever share sale. The offering is also the first IPO from billionaire Mukesh Ambani 's Reliance group in two decades.According to a PTI report, the Jio IPO was fully subscribed within 100 minutes of its opening on October 21.The rapid subscription was notable because large IPOs in India often see a slow start, with institutional investors typically placing their bids closer to the closing deadline. By comparison, the National Stock Exchange of India's share sale recently attracted subscriptions for just 42% of the shares on offer on its first day. Hyundai Motor India's IPO had received bids for only 18% of its offering on the opening day.Also Read | Jio IPO, India’s largest public issue, opens for subscription: Price band, GMP to brokerage views - top 10 things to know The IPO is open to retail investors, employees and eligible Reliance shareholders. The issue will close on Friday, with shares priced in a band of Rs 1,065 to Rs 1,119 apiece.Exchange data showed that institutional investors had bid for 3.25 times the shares reserved for them by Wednesday. Retail participation was lower at that stage, with individual investors applying for 0.22 times their reserved quota.Retail investors have been allocated around one-third of the total offering.The IPO values Jio Platforms at as much as $108.3 billion. Once trading begins on October 28, the company could rank among India's largest listed companies by market capitalisation.Earlier this week, Jio Platforms allotted shares worth $853 million to domestic and international investors, including the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and BlackRock. The anchor investor portion attracted bids exceeding $25 billion, according to a Reuters report.Backed by global investors such as Meta, Google's parent company Alphabet and other institutional investors, Jio Platforms houses India's largest telecom operator. With more than 500 million subscribers, the business is the world's second-largest telecom operator within a single country, behind China Mobile.This is Reliance's first IPO since 2006. Jio Platforms' telecom business, led by Ambani's son Akash, began operations in 2016. Its strategy was built around the expectation that Indians would use the internet much more extensively if access became almost free. By offering inexpensive data and free voice calls, Jio quickly gained market share from competitors such as Bharti Airtel and Vodafone Idea.
Article Summary: Jio IPO was fully subscribed within 100 minutes of its opening on October 21. The rapid subscription was notable because large IPOs in India often see a slow start. The IPO is open to retail investors, employees and eligible Reliance shareholders. The issue will close on Friday, with shares priced in a band of Rs 1,065 to Rs1,119 apiece.

Article Title: LPG consumption down, diesel & petrol sales up in September
Article Text:
LPG consumption in Sept was recorded at 2.6 million tonnes (MT), compared to 2.9 MT during the same month a year earlier

NEW DELHI: LPG demand fell by over 9% year-on-year in Sept, while petrol and diesel sales registered growth of 7% and 5%, respectively, provisional data released by the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) showed.LPG consumption in Sept was recorded at 2.6 million tonnes (MT), compared to 2.9 MT during the same month a year earlier.Month-on-month consumption, however, registered a growth of 8%, up from 2.4 MT.Petrol sales increased from 3.4 MT in Sept last year to 3.6 MT, while diesel consumption rose from 6.8 MT to 7.1 MT. Petrol and diesel consumption had registered year-on-year growth of 7.9% and 6.5%, respectively, in July.While petrol is largely used as an automobile fuel and its consumption is commensurate with the increasing number of vehicles, diesel is consumed by transport vehicles for passenger and freight movement, besides being used in the agricultural sector.Erratic monsoon conditions due to El Nino boosted demand for diesel for irrigation.Cumulative petrol consumption during Apr-Sept in the current financial year increased 7% to 22.6 MT, while diesel consumption rose 4.8% to 47.9 MT. In contrast, LPG consumption declined 14.9% to 13.8 MT from 16.2 MT during the corresponding period of 2025-26.
Article Summary: LPG consumption in Sept was recorded at 2.6 million tonnes (MT), compared to 2.9 MT during the same month a year earlier. Petrol sales increased from 3.4 MT in Sept last year to 3.6 MT, while diesel consumption rose from 6.8 MT to 7.1 MT.

Article Title: Travis Kelce donated $1 million as Pennsylvania food bank funding drops from $4.24 million to $2.69 million
Article Text:
Travis Kelce (Imagn Images)

Travis Kelce's $1 million donation brings relief to Pennsylvania families

Pennsylvania roots inspire another act of generosity

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Long before his wedding celebrations, Travis Kelce made a major contribution to a community that holds a special place in the singer's life. The couple donated $1 million to Helping Harvest Fresh Food Bank in Reading, Pennsylvania, offering timely support as the organisation prepares to help more families than ever. The gift carries a personal connection for Swift, who spent her childhood in the area. It also comes as food banks face rising demand and tighter financial support.The donation arrived at a critical moment for Helping Harvest. The Reading-based food bank expects to distribute a record amount of food this year as more households seek help with everyday grocery costs. Swift and Kelce's contribution could help the organisation purchase supplies, expand its reach and keep essential food available to families facing hardship.For President Jay Worrall, hearing about the couple's generosity was an especially welcome moment. He highlighted Swift's connection to the region and thanked both stars for stepping forward."We were so excited to learn of this unexpected but greatly appreciated donation from a global superstar who grew up right here in our service territory, Taylor Swift , and her fiancé, Travis Kelce," Worrall said in a statement.The gift also comes against a difficult funding backdrop. Helping Harvest received approximately $2.69 million in federal grants for the 2025 fiscal year, compared with around $4.24 million in 2024.That decline makes private contributions increasingly important as the organisation works to meet local needs.Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro's administration also provided $459,000 last year to support a community kitchen. The facility offers culinary training while preparing meals for people who need assistance.Taylor Swift's contribution has a strong hometown connection. Born in West Reading, she spent much of her childhood in nearby Wyomissing before her family moved to Tennessee.
